questions.a: A technical rehearsal that skips from one cue to the next to set timing of lights and sound.

days.guide: Costume parade under lights; note and fix fit/color issues.

questions.q: What do you check in a costume parade?
questions.a: Fit, ability to move, period accuracy, color under the lights, quick-change feasibility.

days.guide: Tech run: full play with all technical elements.

questions.q: What is a stage manager's job during performances?
questions.a: Calling cues, managing backstage, keeping the prompt book, and running the show once the director's work is done.

days.guide: Write production notes and fix issues.

questions.q: What is a call time?
questions.a: The time cast and crew must arrive before a rehearsal or performance.

weeks.assessment_key: Tech run rubric. 4 – All cues executed on time, set/props/costumes complete and functional, production notes documented and addressed, stage manager calls cues confidently. 3 (proficient) – Most cues on time, elements complete, notes written. 2 – Several cue/prop problems. 1 – Not ready.

weeks.prep: All production elements, printed programs, a house manager (family member) for seating, video camera. Plan strike crew assignments.
misconceptions: Skipping notes after the preview audience. Audience reactions reveal timing (laughs, holds).
Breaking character when the audience laughs. Hold for laughs, then continue.
Leaving strike unplanned. Assign who returns what.

days.guide: Full dress rehearsal with timing; give notes.

questions.q: What is 'holding for a laugh'?
questions.a: Pausing in character until the laugh peaks and begins to fade before the next line.

days.guide: Final dress with a preview audience; adjust.

questions.q: Why invite a preview audience?
questions.a: To practice with real reactions and adjust timing and volume.

days.guide: Perform the one-act.

questions.q: What does the house manager do?
questions.a: Manages the audience: seating, tickets/programs, start time, and safety in the house.

days.guide: Second performance; record it.

questions.q: Why is a second performance often stronger?
questions.a: Actors are more relaxed, notes from the first performance are applied, and timing settles.

days.guide: Strike: dismantle set, return materials, clean space.

questions.q: What is strike?
questions.a: Taking down the set and clearing the performance space after the final performance.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric. 4 – Polished production: memorized, clear objectives, consistent blocking, smooth tech, strong pacing and audience connection, professional front-of-house and strike. 3 (proficient) – Memorized, audible, motivated staging, tech mostly smooth. 2 – Noticeable gaps. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Production video, performance journal, headshot photo, résumé template, monologue video, design files, ten-minute play. Prepare the final exam.
misconceptions: Self-critiques that only praise or only criticize. Balance with evidence.
Artistic statements that are generic. Use specific experiences from this year.
Portfolio clutter. Select the best work and label it.

days.guide: Watch the production video; log strengths and growth with timestamps.

questions.q: Name one criterion for evaluating direction.
questions.a: Clarity of story/concept, staging and pictures, pacing, unity of performances and design.

days.guide: Write a 600-word self-critique using criteria.

questions.q: What does a strong self-critique include?
questions.a: A thesis, evaluation of acting, direction, and design with specific moments, and lessons for future work.

days.guide: Write an artistic statement about what theatre means to you.

questions.q: What is an artistic statement?
questions.a: A short first-person statement of an artist's values, approach, and goals.

days.guide: Assemble a digital portfolio: headshot, résumé, monologue video, design work, play.

questions.q: What goes on a theatre résumé?
questions.a: Name and contact, roles with play/company/director, training, special skills.

days.guide: Give the final exam.

questions.q: Name three production roles and their jobs.
questions.a: Director (interpretation and staging), stage manager (calls cues, runs rehearsals/shows), designer (creates set/lights/costumes/sound), house manager (audience).

weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio rubric: proficient = headshot, résumé formatted correctly, monologue video, design samples, ten-minute play, artistic statement, 600-word self-critique — all labeled. Final exam key: 1) Ensemble, yes-and, CROW. 2) Stanislavski: magic if, objective/obstacle/tactic, super-objective, given circumstances. 3) Laban efforts; Viewpoints. 4) Greek: Dionysus, chorus, skene, Antigone. 5) Commedia, Noh, kabuki conventions. 6) Shakespeare: Globe, iambic pentameter. 7) Realism and fourth wall (Ibsen, Chekhov, Glaspell's Trifles). 8) Wilder's Our Town presentational; Stage Manager. 9) Hansberry, Wilson (Century Cycle), Valdez (El Teatro Campesino). 10) Stage types; ground plan; light qualities; costume plot. 11) Freytag's pyramid. 12) Director, stage manager, designers, house manager; cue-to-cue; strike. 90%+ advanced, 75–89% proficient.
